title: multiomeR Manual
text: 1 Introduction

title: multiomeR Manual
text:
1.1 What is multiomeR?
multiomeR is a targets-based workflow for processing and analyzing single-nucleus 10x Genomics Multiome datasets.
The workflow starts from cellranger-arc count outputs, processes RNA and ATAC data, builds multimodal aggregations, and supports optional downstream modules for differential analyses and human genetic enrichment.
multiomeR is currently in beta. It is meant to be adapted to your own data, compute setup, and biological questions, while keeping the shared workflow as lean and readable as possible.

title: multiomeR Manual
text:
1.2 Why use it?

Adaptable framework: The repository is meant to be modified through config files, target selections, helper functions, and optional modules.
Transparent execution: Each processing and analysis step is represented as an explicit targets target.
Efficient reruns: targets reruns only the parts of the workflow affected by changed inputs, code, or config.
Multimodal analysis: The main pipeline covers RNA/ATAC processing, clustering, cell typing, WNN integration, and optional downstream modules.

The framework assumes some familiarity with R and targets, but the public example workflow is intended to provide a concrete starting point.

title: multiomeR Manual
text:
1.3 Terminology
The following nomenclature is used in the documentation and code:

‘10x reaction’ (or possibly just ‘reaction’): The experimental/computational outcome of a single lane on the 10x Genomics Controller chip, which might contain nuclei from multiple samples and/or multiple donors/individuals. One 10x reaction thus corresponds to a single output directory from cellranger-arc count.
donor: A single individual, subject, patient, participant, etc. that has a unique donor_id and specific genotype.
dataset: A group of one or more reactions that share dataset-level processing settings, such as reference genome and reaction-level QC filters.
aggregation: A configured joint analysis of one or more reactions, including merged RNA/ATAC processing, clustering, cell typing, and optional downstream modules.

title: 2  Overview
text:
2.1 How the workflow is organized
multiomeR is organized around one main pipeline and optional downstream modules.
The main pipeline is the workflow most users run first. It starts from cellranger-arc count outputs, processes each 10x reaction, aggregates selected reactions, and builds multimodal RNA/ATAC outputs for clustering, cell typing, and WNN integration.
The modules are optional branches that run from configured aggregations. Enable them only when the relevant input data and biological question are present.

title: 2  Overview
text:
Flowchart of the sample processing pipeline



Main pipeline: Per-reaction QC, dataset-level merging, BPCells-native RNA/ATAC processing, clustering, cell typing, and WNN integration.
Differential analyses: Optional aggregation module for datasets with experimental or phenotypic variables that should be modelled across cell type composition, pseudobulk expression, chromatin accessibility, and TF activity.
Genetic enrichment: Optional human-data module for GWAS-informed chromatin accessibility enrichment and trait-relevance analyses.

title: 3  Quickstart
text:
3.1 1. Prepare the example workflow
This quickstart is the shortest path through the public example workflow. It condenses the detailed Installation, Configuration, and Main pipeline pages into two command blocks.
The downloads include public cellranger-arc count outputs and matching 10x Genomics Cell Ranger ARC reference directories. They are large, and the example workflow can still take substantial time and disk space.
Run these commands in a terminal:
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/koefoeden/multiomeR.git
cd multiomeR

# Install pixi and create the software environment
curl -fsSL https://pixi.sh/install.sh | sh # if pixi is not installed yet
export PATH="$HOME/.pixi/bin:$PATH"
pixi install --run-post-link-scripts

# Download public example inputs
bash example_data/download_10X_cellranger_count_data.sh
bash example_data/download_10X_cellranger_arc_refdata.sh

# Create local config files from templates
cp cfg_datasets_template.yaml cfg_datasets.yaml
cp cfg_aggregations_template.yaml cfg_aggregations.yaml
cp cfg_reactions_template.tsv cfg_reactions.tsv
cp crew_controllers_template.R crew_controllers.R
cp module_differential_analyses/cfg_template.yaml module_differential_analyses/cfg.yaml
cp module_genetic_enrichment/cfg_template.yaml module_genetic_enrichment/cfg.yaml

# Start the interactive R session used below
pixi shell
R
The final two commands start the interactive R session used for the next block.

title: 3  Quickstart
text:
3.2 2. Run the example workflow
Run these commands inside that R session:

# Install GitHub-only R dependencies
remotes::install_github(
  "bnprks/BPCells",
  subdir = "r",
  ref = "28759cdd512578b6cbe549e226e1cd52a2d2308c", # BPCells 0.3.1
  upgrade = "never",
  dependencies = FALSE,
  build_vignettes = FALSE
)
remotes::install_github(
  "stuart-lab/signac",
  ref = "5d66cf6c34322309d5b8aece3fa294f5531b8eee", # Signac 1.9999.4
  upgrade = "never",
  dependencies = FALSE,
  build_vignettes = FALSE
)
remotes::install_github(
  "plger/betterChromVAR",
  ref = "82ae1e4ada8a43c721aa2ae1c3f2c6dfc3d5a637", # betterChromVAR 0.99.41
  upgrade = "never",
  dependencies = FALSE,
  build_vignettes = FALSE
)

# Run the public example targets
targets::tar_make(names = matches("healthy_PBMC_human|blood_human|brain_mouse"))

After the example workflow has completed, see the output gallery for representative outputs.

title: 4  Installation
text:
4.1 Requirements
multiomeR is developed for Linux systems and is managed with pixi. The workflow is not distributed as a conventional installed R package; run it from the repository root so that targets, config files, helper code, and external command-line tools resolve together.
The pixi workspace pins R and most command-line tools in pixi.toml and pixi.lock. The active runtime currently targets R 4.5.x.

title: 4  Installation
text:
A Linux x86_64 machine.
git.
pixi.
Enough disk space for the pixi environment, Cell Ranger outputs, target store, and generated plots.
Input data from cellranger-arc count, or the public example data described in the quickstart.

title: 4  Installation
text:
4.2 Clone the repository

git clone https://github.com/koefoeden/multiomeR.git
cd multiomeR

title: 4  Installation
text:
4.3 Create the pixi environment
If pixi is not installed yet, install it first:

curl -fsSL https://pixi.sh/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.pixi/bin:$PATH"

Install the pixi environment from the repository root:

pixi install --run-post-link-scripts

The --run-post-link-scripts flag is required for Bioconductor data packages such as the BSgenome genome packages. Pixi disables conda post-link scripts by default, but these packages use Bioconda’s post-link scripts to materialize the actual R package directories in the pixi environment.
The pixi environment provides R and the command-line tools used by the workflow, such as bgzip, tabix, macs3, bedGraphToBigWig, bedToBigBed, cellsnp-lite, and vireo.
Start an interactive R session inside the pixi environment:

pixi shell
R

Use this repository-root R session as the evaluation environment for subsequent R commands in this manual.
A small number of R packages still need GitHub versions while upstream conda packages catch up. Install them inside the R session started from the pixi shell:

remotes::install_github(
  "bnprks/BPCells",
  subdir = "r",
  ref = "28759cdd512578b6cbe549e226e1cd52a2d2308c", # BPCells 0.3.1
  upgrade = "never",
  dependencies = FALSE,
  build_vignettes = FALSE
)
remotes::install_github(
  "stuart-lab/signac",
  ref = "5d66cf6c34322309d5b8aece3fa294f5531b8eee", # Signac 1.9999.4
  upgrade = "never",
  dependencies = FALSE,
  build_vignettes = FALSE
)
remotes::install_github(
  "plger/betterChromVAR",
  ref = "82ae1e4ada8a43c721aa2ae1c3f2c6dfc3d5a637", # betterChromVAR 0.99.41
  upgrade = "never",
  dependencies = FALSE,
  build_vignettes = FALSE

text:
4.4 Create local config files
Copy the public templates before constructing the target graph:

cp cfg_datasets_template.yaml cfg_datasets.yaml
cp cfg_reactions_template.tsv cfg_reactions.tsv
cp cfg_aggregations_template.yaml cfg_aggregations.yaml
cp module_differential_analyses/cfg_template.yaml module_differential_analyses/cfg.yaml
cp module_genetic_enrichment/cfg_template.yaml module_genetic_enrichment/cfg.yaml

Edit the copied files when adapting the workflow to your own data. The templates remain available for reference.

title: 4  Installation
text:
4.5 Configure local execution
Create a local controller file before constructing the target graph:

cp crew_controllers_template.R crew_controllers.R

The template uses a local crew controller. Increase workers, cores, and memory only after the example workflow succeeds on your machine.

title: 4  Installation
text:
4.6 Smoke test
After the config files are in place, use the repository-root R session described above to check target graph construction:

targets::tar_manifest(callr_function = NULL)

If this fails, fix the first missing config file, missing command, or missing package reported by the error before running targets::tar_make().

title: 5  Configuration
text:
5.1 Configuring the workflow
After creating local config files during Installation, adapt the workflow by editing the reaction, dataset, aggregation, and optional module config files. These files are the main public interface for changing what the workflow runs.
The terminology is:
YAML entries are divided into two blocks:
Leave the default and example entries available for reference. Add new dataset and aggregation entries for your own data rather than editing target code.

title: 5  Configuration
text:
reaction: one cellranger-arc count output directory from a single 10x reaction.
dataset: a named group of reactions that share reaction-level settings, such as reference genome and QC filters.
aggregation: a configured joint analysis of one or more reactions.



mandatory. Parameters that must be set for the relevant dataset, aggregation, or module.
optional. Parameters with default values, including NULL defaults that intentionally disable optional behavior.

The columns are:







Column
Meaning




reaction_ID
Stable reaction identifier used throughout target names and downstream config.


dataset
Dataset key used to join dataset-level settings from cfg_datasets.yaml.


reaction_donor_id
Donor ID assigned to all nuclei in a non-multiplexed reaction. Use NA for multiplexed reactions.


reaction_n_donors
Number of donors expected in the reaction.


reaction_cellranger_count_dir
Path to the cellranger-arc count output directory.


reaction_cellbender_h5_file
Optional CellBender-corrected GEX H5 file. Use NA when not used.


reaction_donors_VCF_file
Optional VCF for donor demultiplexing. Use NA when not used.



Dataset-level settings live in cfg_datasets.yaml. This is where shared settings for a dataset are defined once and applied to all reactions that reference that dataset in cfg_reactions.tsv.
Typical dataset-level settings include:

dataset_cellranger_arc_refdata_dir: Cell Ranger ARC reference directory for the dataset genome.
dataset_QC_exclude_list_per_reaction: reaction-level QC filters applied before aggregation.

title: 5  Configuration
text:
5.3 Specifying aggregations
Aggregations are configured in cfg_aggregations.yaml. An aggregation is a computational analysis that combines one or more configured reactions and controls the merged RNA/ATAC processing, clustering, annotation, plotting, and optional downstream modules.
At minimum, each aggregation needs:







Field
Meaning




aggregation_reaction_IDs
Reaction IDs from cfg_reactions.tsv to include in the joint analysis.


aggregation_GEX_marker_genes
Named marker-gene lists used for module scoring and cluster annotation.


aggregation_donor_id_metadata_tsv
Donor-level metadata table with a donor_id column.


aggregation_reaction_ID_metadata_tsv
Reaction-level metadata table with a TENX_reaction_ID column.



Optional aggregation settings control QC filters, RNA and ATAC dimensions, clustering resolution, UMAP parameters, subgroup analysis, plotting variables, track export, and enabled modules.
For example, this field enables optional modules for an aggregation:
optional:
  modules: [genetic_enrichment]
Only enable a module when the aggregation has the inputs that module needs.

title: 5  Configuration
text:
5.4 Distributed computing
The pipelines support distributed computing through the targets framework. The active backend is configured in crew_controllers.R, which can be a local symlink or copy.
crew_controllers.R must return a named list with:

controller_list: the list of crew controllers.
controller_resources_tibble: a table with controller_name, cores, RAM_GB, and gpus.

Targets request resources by cores, RAM, and optionally GPUs through get_tar_resources(). The first row of controller_resources_tibble is the default controller, and row order controls which matching controller is preferred. GPU controllers are excluded unless gpus_req > 0.
For local execution, the template copied during Installation is usually sufficient. For cluster execution, adapt crew_controllers.R to match your scheduler, queue names, resource limits, and worker startup requirements.

title: 5  Configuration
text:
5.5 Module configuration
Optional aggregation modules have their own config files:

module_differential_analyses/cfg.yaml
module_genetic_enrichment/cfg.yaml

Only edit module rows for aggregations that enable the corresponding module in cfg_aggregations.yaml.

title: 7  Main pipeline
text:
7.1 Purpose
This workflow is defined in _targets.R and represents the main analysis pipeline after Cell Ranger output generation. It processes individual 10x reactions in parallel, combines selected reactions into aggregations, and builds RNA/ATAC outputs for clustering, cell typing, WNN integration, subgroup reprocessing, and optional downstream modules.
Representative outputs from the public example workflow are collected in the output gallery.

title: 7  Main pipeline
text:
7.2 Inputs
The main pipeline starts from one or more cellranger-arc count output directories. Each configured reaction should point to a directory with the expected outs/ files, including:
<reaction_cellranger_count_dir>/outs/
|-- raw_feature_bc_matrix.h5
|-- filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5
|-- atac_fragments.tsv.gz
|-- atac_fragments.tsv.gz.tbi
|-- atac_possorted_bam.bam
|-- per_barcode_metrics.csv
Reaction-level configuration lives in cfg_reactions.tsv. Start from cfg_reactions_template.tsv, then add one row per 10x reaction with a stable reaction_ID, the matching dataset, the reaction_cellranger_count_dir, and any donor demultiplexing fields relevant to that reaction.
Dataset-level and aggregation-level settings live in cfg_datasets.yaml and cfg_aggregations.yaml. See Configuration for how these files define filtering, aggregation, annotation, and optional module settings.
Each aggregation also points to metadata files:

aggregation_donor_id_metadata_tsv: donor-level metadata with a donor_id column matching the donor IDs assigned during per-reaction processing.
aggregation_reaction_ID_metadata_tsv: reaction-level metadata with a TENX_reaction_ID column matching the configured reaction IDs.

These metadata tables are joined to the per-cell metadata before downstream correction, plotting, and modelling.

title: 7  Main pipeline
text:
7.3 Workflow stages
The main pipeline runs these stages:

per-reaction processing and QC, including optional ambient RNA correction, donor demultiplexing, doublet detection, and barcode filtering
aggregation of selected reactions into dataset-level analysis objects
RNA processing, clustering, marker detection, and cell type annotation
ATAC peak calling, consensus peak construction, chromatin accessibility processing, and chromVAR scoring
WNN integration across RNA and ATAC modalities
optional subgroup reprocessing for sufficiently large parent groups

text:
7.8 Running the pipeline
From the repository-root R session described in Installation, run the main workflow in checkpoint-sized pieces. Replace your_aggregation with the aggregation name from cfg_aggregations.yaml, for example blood_human.

targets::tar_make(
  names = targets::tar_described_as(tidyselect::contains("checkpoint:GEX")) &
    tidyselect::matches("your_aggregation")
)

At the GEX checkpoint, inspect the aggregation-level barcode exclusion summaries, RNA-only QC plots, marker summaries, and GEX_Seurat_object.your_aggregation. If the GEX filtering, clustering, and annotation look acceptable, continue to the multimodal checkpoint:

targets::tar_make(
  names = targets::tar_described_as(tidyselect::contains("checkpoint:multimodal")) &
    tidyselect::matches("your_aggregation")
)

At the multimodal checkpoint, inspect the ATAC QC plots, peak and motif summaries, WNN UMAPs, modality-weight plots, and multimodal_Seurat_object.your_aggregation. If the aggregation enables the optional downstream modules, continue with their checkpoint outputs:

targets::tar_make(
  names = targets::tar_described_as(tidyselect::contains("checkpoint:differential_analyses")) &
    tidyselect::matches("your_aggregation")
)

targets::tar_make(
  names = targets::tar_described_as(tidyselect::contains("checkpoint:genetic_enrichment")) &
    tidyselect::matches("your_aggregation")
)

To run all configured aggregations for a checkpoint, omit the & tidyselect::matches("your_aggregation") part. To run the full workflow after checkpoint review, run:

targets::tar_make()

The full main pipeline can be computationally expensive. Start with the public example or a narrow target selection, then scale to larger datasets after local paths, metadata files, and controller settings are working.

title: 8  Differential analyses module
text:
8.1 Purpose
This optional module is relevant when an aggregation has experimental, clinical, phenotypic, or technical variables that should be modelled across processed Multiome data. It is defined inside the root _targets.R workflow, with module-specific target fragments and configuration in module_differential_analyses/.
The module can model:
Representative outputs from this module are shown in the output gallery.
Enable the module for an aggregation in cfg_aggregations.yaml, then configure the module-specific model settings in module_differential_analyses/cfg.yaml. See Configuration for the general config workflow.

title: 8  Differential analyses module
text:
differential cell type composition using generalized linear mixed models
differential gene expression on pseudobulked RNA counts
differential chromatin accessibility on pseudobulked ATAC counts
differential transcription factor activity using chromVAR-derived pseudobulk signals

8.4 Running the pipeline
From the repository-root R session described in Installation, run the relevant root workflow targets. Replace your_aggregation with an aggregation that enables the module in cfg_aggregations.yaml.

targets::tar_make(names = matches("your_aggregation"))

Runtime depends on the number of modelled variables, cell types, donors, and pseudobulk contrasts in the aggregation.

title: 9  Genetic enrichment module
text:
9.1 Purpose
This optional module is relevant for human-data aggregations where GWAS or fine-mapped trait evidence should be integrated with chromatin accessibility data. It is defined inside the root _targets.R workflow, with module-specific target fragments and configuration in module_genetic_enrichment/.
The module can identify trait-relevant cell types and regulatory programs using:
Representative outputs from this module are shown in the output gallery.
Enable the module for a human-data aggregation in cfg_aggregations.yaml, then configure Open Targets studies and module-specific settings in module_genetic_enrichment/cfg.yaml. See Configuration for the general config workflow.
